definition: The tiny building block that all substances are made of. An atom has a nucleus with protons and neutrons, and electrons in shells outside it.
The centre of the atom. The protons and neutrons are found here, along with almost all of the atom's mass.
A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus. The number of protons decides which element the atom is.
A particle in the atomic nucleus that has no charge.
A negatively charged particle that moves outside the nucleus, in electron shells. An atom has as many electrons as protons.
The layers where the electrons are found. The inner shell holds 2 electrons and the next shell holds 8. The outer shell decides how the atom bonds.
A substance that is made of only one kind of atom, for example hydrogen, carbon, oxygen or iron. There are 118 known elements.
The number of protons in the atomic nucleus. It decides which element it is and where the atom belongs in the periodic table.
The short form of an element's name: a capital letter, sometimes followed by a small letter (H, C, N, O, Cl). The symbols are international.
A group of atoms that are joined together by chemical bonds. The atoms can be from the same element (O₂) or from different elements (H₂O).
What holds atoms together in a molecule. Two atoms share electrons, and in a structural formula a shared pair is drawn as a line.
A bond where two atoms share one pair of electrons. It is drawn as one line, for example H–H.
A bond where two atoms share two pairs of electrons. It is drawn as two lines, for example O=O in oxygen gas.
A bond where two atoms share three pairs of electrons. It is drawn as three lines, for example N≡N in nitrogen gas.
An element whose atoms have a full outer shell and therefore do not bond to other atoms, for example helium, neon and argon.
A substance whose atoms come from at least two different elements, for example water (H₂O) and carbon dioxide (CO₂).
Several substances that are together without reacting with each other, for example air. The substances can be separated without a chemical reaction.
Shows which atoms a molecule has and how many of each, for example H₂O or CO₂.
A drawing that shows how the atoms in a molecule are joined together. A single bond is drawn with one line, a double bond with two and a triple bond with three.
The small number after a chemical symbol. It tells you how many atoms of that kind there are in one molecule. H₂O has 2 H and 1 O.
The large number in front of a formula. It tells you how many molecules there are. 2 H₂O is two water molecules.
A change where bonds are broken and new bonds are formed, so that new substances are made. The atoms change partners but never disappear.
A substance you start with in a chemical reaction. The reactants are on the left of the arrow.
A substance that is formed in a chemical reaction. The products are on the right of the arrow.
A reaction formula where there are the same number of atoms of each kind on both sides of the arrow. You balance it by changing the large numbers, never the subscripts.
A change where the molecules of the substance stay the same and only the substance's shape or state changes, for example when water boils. No new substances are formed.
